questions.q: s = 4, 6, 8, 10. What is s.shift(1).rolling(2).mean() at the last row?
questions.why: After shift(1): NaN, 4, 6, 8. The last two values are 6 and 8. Mean = 7.

questions.q: s = 4, 6, 8, 10. What is s.rolling(2).mean() at the last row?
questions.why: Rolling(2) uses 8 and 10. Mean = 9. It contains the current value 10, so it leaks.

questions.q: A table has many products stacked in long format. You write df['lag_1'] = df['sales'].shift(1). What is wrong?
options: The first row of each product gets the last value of the previous product
shift does not work on tables
why: The lags would cross product borders.
shift works on Series and DataFrames.

questions.q: You have a direct model for horizon 14 (target = value 14 days after the origin). Counting lags back from the origin, which feature is allowed?
options: Average of the 7 days after the origin
why: Correct: the origin day is known when the forecast is made.
That day is in the future at the origin.
These days are in the future too.

questions.q: A model has an amazing score. A colleague finds the feature `price_mean_7d = price.rolling(7, center=True).mean()`. What is the most likely issue?
options: The centered window uses future prices, which are not known at forecast time
why: Scaling would not make a model suspiciously good.
Correct: half of the window lies after the current time.
The number of rows is not the issue.
